newsitem.title: USA: US spending seen up, not hiking growth - Fed source.
newsitem.headline: US spending seen up, not hiking growth - Fed source.

text.p: U.S. consumers are likely to spend more in the third quarter than they did in the second, but the expansion in consumption is not expected to bring overall economic growth to worrisome, above-trend levels, a Federal Reserve source said.
"I think the third quarter will almost certainly be a better quarter than the second one as far as consumer spending goes," the Fed source told Reuters on Tuesday.
"(But) just because consumption would pick up, that doesn't necessarily imply that the whole economy would move above trend," the source added.

The Fed source said the U.S. economy is likely to grow moderately over the next few quarters, with an annualized Gross Domestic Product (GDP) rate of growth between the perceived potential trend of 2.0 and 2.5 percent.
"We had a slowing in the second quarter; and generally speaking, our view is that we're going to continue around the current pace ... until the end of this year," the source said.

Fears that economic growth could move back above the trend levels of the second quarter and, as a result, prompt the Fed to tighten monetary policy have roiled financial markets recently, sending the yield on the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond above 6.60 percent from a recent low of 6.36 percent.
The Fed source declined to make specific comments about the current level of interest rates or the future of the nation's monetary policy.

The source said one of the reasons why consumer spending alone was not likely to boost overall growth was that the strong investment level seen in several areas of the economy in the first half of the year was unlikely to continue.
"There are other places in the economy where there was very strong investment ... that seem unlikely to be sustainable going further out," the source said.
The Fed source said inflation remains "very low," with few signs of major upward pressures at this point.

But the source said he was still in the agnostic camp about the so-called "new economy theory," which preaches that higher productivity and rising foreign competition will put a more permanent lid on inflation.
"If indeed productivity is stronger than the numbers suggest, that would provide (an answer to the question of) why we have low inflation and why we have a strong stock market," the source said.
Commonenting on the status of the nation's labor market, the Fed source said it remains "very tight".

Asked if the jobless rate, currently at 4.8 percent, could drop even further without triggering inflation, the source said: "If the economy were to grow at roughly 2.0 percent, then I think that would imply that unemployment stays roughly where it is now."

The source then added: "Now if you're asking if we could lower the unemployment rate even further without triggering higher inflation, then my guess is probably not. Though ... we have been surprised about that already."

The Federal Reserve will meet to deliberate on the nation's monetary policy on August 19. The Fed last raised rates on March 25, when it hiked the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to the current 5.50 percent.
The central bank stood pat in the May and July meetings of its policy-setting body, the Federal Open Market Committee.
A large majority of pundits and Fed watchers on Wall Street expect the Fed to keep monetary policy unchanged during its next meeting in August.
